title: Node.js Fundamentals Quiz
description: Test your Node.js knowledge: event loop, garbage collection, streams, V8 internals and more.

questions.text: Node.js is described as 'single-threaded'. What does this primarily mean in the context of JavaScript execution?

options.text: It can only handle one HTTP request at a time
JavaScript code runs on a single call stack in one thread
It uses only one CPU core for all operations
It cannot run multiple Node.js processes on the same machine

questions.explanation: Node.js executes JavaScript on a single call stack (the main thread), but delegates I/O to libuv's thread pool, enabling non-blocking concurrency.

questions.text: What does `require('fs')` do in a Node.js module?

options.text: Fetches the 'fs' package from the npm registry at runtime
Loads and caches the built-in file system module, returning its exports object
Creates a new file system instance for the current module only
Registers a file system event listener on the process object

questions.explanation: `require()` looks up the module in the cache, or loads it from disk and compiles it, then returns its `module.exports` object — subsequent calls return the cached copy.

questions.text: Which field in `package.json` specifies the entry point file that Node.js loads when your package is `require()`-d?

options.text: start
index
main
entry

questions.explanation: The `main` field in `package.json` points to the file Node.js resolves when another module requires your package; it defaults to `index.js` if omitted.

questions.text: What is the key difference between `fs.readFileSync()` and `fs.readFile()` in Node.js?

options.text: `readFileSync` reads larger files; `readFile` is limited to 1 MB
`readFileSync` blocks the event loop until the file is read; `readFile` is non-blocking and uses a callback
`readFile` is deprecated; `readFileSync` is the modern API
They are identical — the 'Sync' suffix is cosmetic

questions.explanation: `readFileSync` blocks the entire event loop until the read completes, while `readFile` hands the I/O to libuv and invokes the callback when done.

questions.text: In Node.js, what is a callback?

options.text: A built-in error type for async failures
A function passed as an argument to another function, invoked when an async operation completes
A synchronous wrapper around a Promise
A special method on the EventEmitter class

questions.explanation: The callback pattern is Node's foundational async primitive — you pass a function that Node calls back with `(error, result)` once the operation finishes.

questions.text: How do you read an environment variable named `PORT` in a Node.js process?

options.text: `env.get('PORT')`
`process.env.PORT`
`os.env('PORT')`
`global.PORT`

questions.explanation: `process.env` is an object populated from the process's environment variables; accessing `process.env.PORT` returns its string value or `undefined`.

questions.text: Which built-in Node.js module would you use to join two path segments in a cross-platform safe way?

options.text: `fs`
`url`
`path`
`os`

questions.explanation: The `path` module provides `path.join()` and `path.resolve()`, which handle platform-specific separators (`/` vs `\`) automatically.

questions.text: What does `npm run build` execute?

options.text: Downloads and installs all packages listed in `dependencies`
Runs the `build` script defined under the `scripts` key in `package.json`
Compiles all `.ts` files to `.js` using Node's built-in compiler
Creates a production bundle and uploads it to npm

questions.explanation: `npm run <name>` executes the shell command mapped to that name in the `scripts` section of `package.json`, with `node_modules/.bin` added to PATH.

questions.text: In a Node.js stack trace, what does the line `at Object.<anonymous> (app.js:42:15)` tell you?

options.text: An anonymous object was exported from `app.js`
The error originated at line 42, column 15 of `app.js`
The file `app.js` has 42 exports
Process memory usage at the time of the error

questions.explanation: Each stack frame shows the function name, file, line number, and column number, letting you pinpoint exactly where in source the call was made.

questions.text: Which of the following is available in a browser's JavaScript runtime but NOT in Node.js by default?

options.text: `setTimeout`
`Promise`
`window`
`Array.prototype.map`

questions.explanation: The `window` global (and browser-specific APIs like `document`, `localStorage`) do not exist in Node.js; Node has `global`, `process`, and its own I/O APIs instead.

options.text: D → A → B → C
D → C → A → B
D → C → B → A
A → B → C → D

questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (D), then microtasks/nextTick queue (C), then the timers phase fires setTimeout (A), and finally the check phase fires setImmediate (B) — but within the I/O context setTimeout(0) vs setImmediate order is non-deterministic outside I/O; in a top-level script the most common observed order is D→C→A→B or D→C→B→A.

questions.text: In what phase of the Node.js event loop does `setImmediate()` fire?

options.text: Timers phase
Poll phase
Check phase
Close callbacks phase

questions.explanation: The event loop phases are: timers → pending callbacks → idle/prepare → poll → check → close callbacks; `setImmediate` callbacks run in the **check** phase.

questions.text: Which of the following has the highest execution priority in Node.js's async scheduling?

options.text: `setTimeout(fn, 0)`
`setImmediate(fn)`
`process.nextTick(fn)`
Resolved `Promise` `.then()` callbacks

questions.explanation: `process.nextTick` callbacks drain completely before any microtask (Promise) callbacks, which themselves drain before the next event loop phase begins.

questions.text: What type of Node.js stream would you use to both read from and write to, AND transform the data in transit (e.g., a gzip compressor)?

options.text: Readable stream
Writable stream
Duplex stream
Transform stream

questions.explanation: A Transform stream is a Duplex where output is computed from input — `zlib.createGzip()` is the canonical example; a plain Duplex has independent read/write sides.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of the Node.js `cluster` module?

options.text: To distribute npm packages across multiple machines
To fork multiple worker processes that share the same server port, utilizing multiple CPU cores
To spawn child processes that run independent scripts with no shared state
To create thread pools for CPU-intensive synchronous tasks

questions.explanation: The `cluster` module forks child processes (all sharing port 80 via the OS round-robin or the master passing handles), letting a Node app scale across CPU cores.

questions.text: How does `worker_threads` differ from `child_process` in Node.js?

options.text: `worker_threads` share memory via `SharedArrayBuffer`; `child_process` spawns fully isolated OS processes
`child_process` is faster for CPU tasks because it uses native threads
`worker_threads` cannot communicate with the main thread
They are interchangeable; the names are aliases

questions.explanation: Worker threads run in the same process and can share memory (SharedArrayBuffer/Atomics), while child_process forks separate OS processes with isolated V8 heaps.

questions.text: In V8's heap layout, what is the 'New Space' (Young Generation) used for?

options.text: Storing compiled machine code for JIT-compiled functions
Short-lived objects that are expected to be collected quickly
Large objects over 1 MB that cannot fit in regular pages
The call stack and local variable frames

questions.explanation: V8 divides the heap into New Space (young/short-lived objects collected by Scavenge) and Old Space (long-lived objects collected by Mark-Sweep/Mark-Compact).

questions.text: When a Node.js module is `require()`-d a second time, what happens?

options.text: The module file is re-read from disk and re-executed
An error is thrown to prevent duplicate initialization
The cached `exports` object from the first load is returned immediately
A new isolated module instance is created

questions.explanation: Node's module system stores each resolved module in `require.cache`; subsequent `require()` calls for the same file return the cached `exports` without re-executing the module code.

questions.text: Which `EventEmitter` method registers a listener that fires only once and then automatically removes itself?

options.text: `emitter.on(event, listener)`
`emitter.once(event, listener)`
`emitter.addOnceListener(event, listener)`
`emitter.emit(event, { once: true })`

questions.explanation: `emitter.once()` wraps the listener so it deregisters itself after the first emission, preventing repeated calls without manual `removeListener` cleanup.

questions.text: What is libuv's role in Node.js?

options.text: It is the JavaScript engine that compiles and executes JS code
It provides the cross-platform async I/O event loop, thread pool, and OS abstraction layer
It manages npm package downloads and caching
It implements the HTTP/2 protocol for Node's `http2` module

questions.explanation: libuv is the C library underneath Node.js that implements the event loop, thread pool (for file I/O, DNS, etc.), and platform-specific networking abstractions.

questions.text: Which garbage collection algorithm does V8 use for the Young Generation (New Space)?

options.text: Mark-Sweep
Mark-Compact
Scavenge (Cheney's semi-space copying)
Reference counting

questions.explanation: V8 uses Scavenge — a semi-space copying collector — for the Young Generation because most objects die young, making evacuation of survivors fast.

questions.text: Why can a full Mark-Compact GC cycle cause observable latency spikes in a Node.js server?

options.text: It temporarily doubles memory usage by copying the entire heap
It runs stop-the-world pauses while compacting the Old Space, blocking the event loop
It recompiles all JIT-optimized functions to free code cache memory
It flushes the libuv thread pool and restarts all pending I/O operations

questions.explanation: Mark-Compact requires stop-the-world (STW) pauses to safely move objects and update all pointers, during which the event loop cannot process new requests.

questions.text: You run `node --prof app.js` and then `node --prof-process isolate-*.log`. What kind of output does this produce?

options.text: A heap snapshot in JSON format compatible with Chrome DevTools
A human-readable statistical CPU profile showing hot functions and their call percentages
A timeline of all GC pauses with their durations in milliseconds
A network waterfall diagram of all HTTP requests made during the run

questions.explanation: `--prof` generates a V8 tick-based sampling profile; `--prof-process` post-processes it into a report showing which functions consumed the most CPU time.

questions.text: Which of the following patterns is the most common cause of memory leaks in long-running Node.js servers?

options.text: Using `const` instead of `let` for module-level variables
Accumulating listeners on an EventEmitter without ever calling `removeListener`
Calling `JSON.parse` on large strings repeatedly
Using `async/await` instead of raw callbacks

questions.explanation: Each `emitter.on()` call adds a reference that prevents GC of the listener and anything it closes over; without cleanup they accumulate indefinitely, a classic Node.js leak pattern.

questions.text: What does the Node.js flag `--max-old-space-size=4096` control?

options.text: The maximum number of files that can be open simultaneously
The size of libuv's thread pool in megabytes
The upper limit of V8's Old Space heap in megabytes before OOM is thrown
The maximum allowed size of a single JSON payload parsed with `JSON.parse`

questions.explanation: `--max-old-space-size` sets the maximum heap size for V8's Old Generation; exceeding it triggers a final GC and then throws a fatal out-of-memory error.

questions.text: A synchronous CPU-bound loop running for 2 seconds is accidentally placed in an HTTP request handler. What is the most accurate description of the impact?

options.text: Only that specific request is delayed; other requests continue normally
The event loop poll phase is blocked for 2 seconds, stalling ALL other incoming requests and timers
Node automatically offloads the loop to libuv's thread pool to prevent blocking
The cluster master process detects the block and restarts the worker

questions.explanation: JavaScript is single-threaded; a synchronous CPU loop occupies the entire event loop, preventing any I/O callbacks, timers, or new requests from being processed until it finishes.

questions.text: What is back-pressure in Node.js streams, and what role does `highWaterMark` play?

options.text: Back-pressure is an HTTP rate-limit; `highWaterMark` sets the requests-per-second ceiling
Back-pressure is the signal that a writable stream's buffer is full; `highWaterMark` sets the buffer size threshold at which `write()` returns `false`
Back-pressure is a V8 GC pause; `highWaterMark` triggers early GC when heap exceeds this fraction
Back-pressure is unused in Node.js streams; it is only relevant to TCP sockets

questions.explanation: When a Writable's internal buffer exceeds `highWaterMark` bytes, `write()` returns `false` (back-pressure signal); producers should pause until the `drain` event fires to avoid unbounded memory growth.

questions.text: What is the primary advantage of N-API (now Node-API) over previous native addon interfaces?

options.text: It allows writing native addons in Python instead of C/C++
It provides an ABI-stable interface so native addons do not need to be recompiled for every new Node.js version
It gives native addons direct access to V8's garbage collector to manage their own memory
It automatically parallelizes native addon execution across all CPU cores

questions.explanation: N-API exposes a stable ABI layer that abstracts V8 internals, meaning a native addon compiled once works across Node.js major versions without recompilation.

questions.text: How do V8 'hidden classes' (also called 'shapes' or 'maps') improve JavaScript object performance?

options.text: They compress object keys using a dictionary to reduce memory per object
They allow V8 to generate optimized machine code by tracking object property layouts and reusing them across instances with the same shape
They hide private class fields from the garbage collector to prevent premature collection
They pre-allocate a fixed heap page per constructor function

questions.explanation: V8 assigns a hidden class (shape/map) to each object based on its property layout; objects sharing the same shape can share JIT-compiled inline caches, enabling fast property access.

questions.text: When using PM2 to achieve zero-downtime restarts (`pm2 reload`), what mechanism does PM2 use?

options.text: It pauses the load balancer, restarts all workers simultaneously, then resumes traffic
It creates a new worker, waits for it to signal readiness, routes traffic to it, then gracefully kills the old worker — one at a time
It patches the running process in memory without spawning a new one
It relies on the OS kernel's live-patching feature to swap code pages atomically

questions.explanation: PM2 reload performs a rolling restart: it spawns a new worker, waits for it to emit `process.send('ready')`, moves traffic to it, then gracefully shuts down the old worker — ensuring zero downtime.

tiers.label: Node.js Legend
tiers.description: Outstanding work — you have a deep mastery of Node.js internals. You understand exactly how the event loop phases interact, why process.nextTick drains before Promises, and how V8's Scavenge and Mark-Compact collectors affect latency. You can diagnose memory leaks caused by retained listeners, tune heap sizes with --max-old-space-size, and design back-pressure-aware stream pipelines. Your knowledge of N-API, hidden classes, and PM2 zero-downtime reloads puts you firmly in the top tier of Node.js engineers. Whether you are profiling CPU hot paths with --prof or architecting cluster-based multi-core servers, you do it with confidence.

tiers.label: Node.js Expert
tiers.description: Great performance — you have a solid command of Node.js beyond the basics. You are comfortable with the event loop phases, understand the difference between setImmediate and process.nextTick, and can reason about stream types and back-pressure. You know how the cluster module distributes connections and how worker_threads differ from child_process. A few advanced V8 internals and GC details are still areas to sharpen, but your foundation is strong and you are well-equipped to build and debug production Node.js applications.
tiers.shareText: I scored Expert on the Node.js Fundamentals Quiz at ToolNotch!

tiers.label: Node.js Practitioner
tiers.description: Good effort — you have a working knowledge of Node.js fundamentals. You understand the single-threaded model, how require works, and the basics of async patterns. Some of the deeper topics — event loop phases, V8 heap segments, stream back-pressure — are areas where more study will pay off. Reading the official Node.js documentation on the event loop and spending time with the stream and cluster modules will help you level up to Expert and beyond.
tiers.shareText: I took the Node.js Fundamentals Quiz at ToolNotch and scored Practitioner level!

tiers.label: Node.js Rookie
tiers.description: You are just getting started with Node.js, and that is perfectly fine — everyone begins somewhere. Focus on the core concepts first: the single-threaded event loop, how require and module.exports work, the difference between synchronous and asynchronous file I/O, and how to use process.env for configuration. Once those are solid, explore callbacks and Promises, then move on to streams and the cluster module. With consistent practice and the right resources, you will be moving up the tiers quickly.
